Potentia Ordinata
pō-ten´shĭ-ă ôr-dĭ-nā´tă
n. phrase (Latin: God's ordained power; what He has actually willed and bound Himself to do in this world)
Latin ordinata, set in order, from ordo. The same power as absoluta, now considered as God has actually arranged the world, the covenant, and the means. Not a second power. A second way of speaking of one power.

Biblical Definition

Potentia ordinata is the power God has actually put to work. He does not merely possess might. He has taken counsel and will perform it: “My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). He has sworn and will not repent: “The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psa 110:4). The gospel itself is an ordained thing: “Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain” (Act 2:23). And the blessing is not a mood. It is a word God will not unsay: “For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath” (Heb 6:16–17). The ordained power is why a sinner may rest. God has not left Himself loose options against His own promise.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin pair. Potentia ordinata is the scholastic name for God's power as He has actually bound it to the decree, the covenant, and the sworn word.

POTENTIA ORDINATA, Latin, ordained power. Scholastic theological phrase, not an 1828 English headword.

God's power considered as He has actually willed this world, this covenant, these means.

Not a weaker power than the absolute. The same power, now pledged.

The ground of assurance: what God has sworn, He will perform.

Key Scripture

Isa 46:10 — "Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:"

Psa 110:4 — "The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

Act 2:23 — "Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:"

Heb 6:17 — "Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:"

Psa 115:3 — "But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased."

Modern Corruption

Ordained power is treated as a cage God is stuck in, and Scripture treats it as a counsel He freely bound with an oath.

expand to see more

Process theology and its softer cousins hear “ordained” as if God had been overtaken by the world He made and must now cope. Isaiah 46:10 is the opposite sentence. My counsel shall stand. I will do all my pleasure. The order is His pleasure executed, not His defeat managed. A God who is learning the plot with us is not the God who delivered the Son by determinate counsel.

The other corruption is pastoral despair dressed as humility: perhaps God has reserved a private will against the promise, and the gospel is what He says in public. Hebrews 6 was written to kill that thought. He confirmed the counsel by an oath, that by two immutable things we might have strong consolation. The ordained power is not a threat behind the offer. It is the offer made unbreakable.

Acts 2:23 holds the pair the schools were trying to name. Determinate counsel and wicked hands in one verse. God ordained the cross. Men meant it for evil. The ordained power does not excuse the hands. It does mean the hands did not surprise Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin potentia ordinata; Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel; Greek boule (G1012), counsel, purpose.

Latin potentia ordinata — power as bound to the order God has set.

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel; Isaiah 46:10, my counsel shall stand.

Greek boule (G1012) — counsel; Acts 2:23, determinate counsel; Hebrews 6:17, immutability of his counsel.

Usage

"“My counsel shall stand” — ordained is not trapped."

"“Confirmed it by an oath” — so the heirs would stop guessing."

"“Determinate counsel” — and wicked hands in the same sentence."
